claims.text: The candidate Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloys and selected quaternary and ternary subsets have nominally single-phase FCC microstructures after standard thermomechanical processing.
Atomic short-range order governs mechanical-property differences in single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-based alloys and their subsets.
Atomic short-range order alters local lattice distortions.
SRO-induced lattice distortions modify dislocation nucleation, pinning, and mobility.
Annealing at 600–800°C for variable times followed by rapid quenching can systematically alter SRO without changing overall composition.
Atom probe tomography, high-resolution TEM, and diffraction can quantify the relevant nanoscale SRO.
The nanoscale chemical ordering modulates local lattice-distortion fields.
Higher SRO creates more effective dislocation-pinning centers.
More effective dislocation pinning increases yield strength.
Lower SRO facilitates easier dislocation glide and greater ductility.
Treatments that enhance SRO will increase yield strength relative to the as-processed equiatomic quinary baseline.
Treatments that enhance SRO will produce a distinct strain-hardening profile relative to the quinary baseline.
Treatments that enhance SRO will reduce ductility relative to the quinary baseline.
Measured SRO parameters will correlate systematically and quantitatively with yield strength, strain hardening, and ductility.
The as-processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni FCC alloy has an equilibrium level of SRO.
The proposed mechanism is intended primarily for single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys within controlled thermomechanical-processing windows.
Residual stresses, compositional fluctuations, and other microstructural features may overlap with or confound the influence of SRO.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as both merely as-processed and as having an equilibrium SRO level; standard thermomechanical processing does not by itself establish that the retained SRO is at equilibrium.
